newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe minister says strikers have political aim.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe minister says strikers have political aim.

text.p: The Zimbabwean government accused its political opponents on Monday of organising a current strike by nurses and doctors to challenge its authority.

Acting Public Service, Labour and Social Welfare Minister Nathan Shamuyarira told state media a mass demonstration called for later on Monday by trade unions, churches and human rights groups to press the government to resolve the costly strike was part of this campaign.
"All the known opposition parties are supporting and helping to organise it. The organisers are seeking a political objective," he charged, arguing the strikers deserved no public sympathy.
The organisers were not available for immediate comment.

President Robert Mugabe -- in power for the last 16 years and whose ruling ZANU-PF party currently holds 147 seats in Zimbabwe's 150-member parliament -- has ruled the southern African state with little challenge from a weak and fragmented opposition.
Political analysts say both Mugabe and ZANU-PF, who deny the charges, have become arrogant and insensitive over the years.

The Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU), the Zimbabwe Human Rights Organisation (Zimrights) and the Zimbabwe Council of Churches (ZCC) said on Friday they hoped to break the government's hardline stance against the striking nurses and doctors through mass demonstrations starting on Monday.
"In participating in the demonstration(s), they need to be very clear that they are taking a political position," Shamuyarira said, vowing the government would not back down on the issue.
The three-week strike by state nurses, who were joined last week by doctors, has crippled Zimbabwe's public health system and led to the closure of the country's two largest hospitals.

Union officials say 10,000 of 14,000 nurses employed in state hospitals and 500 of 800 doctors in these institutions are on strike, but Shamuyarira said on Monday only 1,000 nurses and 100 doctors were involved.

He said the government was willing to discuss the strikers' grievances over pay and working conditions but would not submit to blackmail, reiterating that it would not reverse its decision to fire all strikers.
He said the government would not reverse its decision to fire all strikers, saying it was advertising for nurses and doctors in Britain, South Africa and other African states to replace those sacked.
